summary.text: The triple point of a substance is the single temperature and pressure at which its solid, liquid and gas phases can all coexist in equilibrium.
On a phase diagram it is where the sublimation, fusion and vaporisation curves meet; for water it lies at 273.16 K and a vapor pressure of about 611.657 pascals.
Triple-point cells give highly precise, repeatable temperatures, so they are used to calibrate thermometers and to anchor the ITS-90 temperature scale.

facts.label: Old SI role
facts.value: Water's triple point defined the kelvin until 2019

facts.label: Water under pressure
facts.value: 15 known ice phases with several triple points

items.prompt: A chunk of ice floats in the near-vacuum of outer space, at a pressure far below water's triple point, and is warmed. What happens to it?

options.label: It melts into liquid water, then boils away
It turns straight into vapor without becoming liquid
It stays solid no matter how much it is warmed
It shatters into smaller pieces of ice

items.explain: Below the triple point pressure liquid water cannot exist, so ice sublimates directly into vapor when heated.

items.prompt: A lab wants a thermometer checked against a temperature that can be reproduced exactly every time. What makes a sealed cell of pure water suitable?

options.label: Water boils at the same temperature everywhere on Earth
Pure water never freezes, so it stays steady
Ice, water and vapor coexist only at one fixed point
Water's temperature is set by the lab's air pressure

items.explain: Solid, liquid and gas coexist only at the triple point, which gives a highly precise, reproducible temperature.

items.prompt: On a phase diagram, three curves, for sublimation, fusion and vaporisation, all meet at one spot. What is that spot called?

options.label: The triple point
The critical point
The Curie point
The lambda point

items.explain: The triple point is where the sublimation, fusion and vaporisation curves meet.

items.prompt: For most substances, liquid cannot exist below the temperature of the gas-liquid-solid triple point, but water is an exception. What is different about water?

options.label: Water has no solid phase at ordinary pressures
Water vapor turns directly into liquid at any cold temperature
Water's triple point lies at a much higher pressure
The melting point of ordinary ice falls as pressure rises

items.explain: Because ice's melting point decreases with pressure, liquid water can exist below the triple point temperature when compressed.

items.prompt: Triple-point cells for water use a set isotope mix rather than any natural sample. Why?

options.label: Different isotope mixes shift the triple point slightly
Natural isotopes make the water freeze too quickly
A set mix keeps the water from becoming a gas
Isotopes of water change the pressure of the room

items.explain: Variations in isotopic composition cause small changes in the triple point, so a specific composition is used.

items.prompt: Today the kelvin is fixed through the Boltzmann constant. What does that make water's triple point?

options.label: Still the exact definition of one kelvin
A measured value that matters but no longer defines the unit
A temperature that no longer has any use
A value that is now defined as 273 K exactly

items.explain: After the 2019 revision the triple point of water is no longer a defining point, though its empirical value remains important.

paragraphs.heading: Three phases at once
paragraphs.text: A substance's triple point is the pair of temperature and pressure values where its gas, liquid and solid forms can all exist together in thermodynamic equilibrium. It is the spot where three curves meet: the sublimation curve, the fusion curve and the vaporisation curve. Mercury, for example, reaches its triple point at −38.8 °C and a pressure of 0.165 mPa.

paragraphs.heading: Not always gas, liquid and solid
paragraphs.text: Some triple points do not involve a gas at all. Substances that have several solid forms, called polymorphs, can have triple points where more than one solid phase takes part. Helium-4 is an odd case: it has no sublimation curve, so it has no triple point where its solid meets its gas. It has four other special points instead: one where vapor, liquid and superfluid meet, one for solid, liquid and superfluid, one with two solids and a liquid, and one with two solids and a superfluid. None of these is the lambda point, which is not a triple point of any kind.

paragraphs.heading: A yardstick for temperature
paragraphs.text: The term was first used on August 3, 1871, by James Thomson, the brother of Lord Kelvin. Triple points of several substances now fix points on ITS-90, the international temperature scale, from hydrogen at 13.8033 K up to water at 273.16 K, or 0.01 °C. Until 2019, water's triple point also defined the kelvin, the SI base unit of thermodynamic temperature, by being set at exactly 273.16 K. The 2019 revision of the SI instead fixed the Boltzmann constant at exactly 1.380649×10⁻²³ J⋅K⁻¹. Since then, water's triple point has been a measured value rather than a defining one.

paragraphs.heading: Water at its triple point
paragraphs.text: Water's triple point still matters in practice. Ice, liquid water and water vapour sit together in stable balance at about 273.16 K and a vapour pressure of 611.657 pascals. Liquid water needs at least that pressure to exist. Below it, as in the vacuum of outer space, ice heated at constant pressure sublimates, turning straight into vapour. Above it, heated ice first melts into liquid at a constant temperature and then evaporates or boils at a higher temperature.

paragraphs.heading: Where water breaks the rule
paragraphs.text: In most substances, the lowest temperature at which a liquid can exist is the gas–liquid–solid triple point, but water is different. The melting point of ordinary ice falls as the pressure rises. Also, just below the triple point, squeezing water vapour at a fixed temperature turns it first into ice and then into liquid. At high pressures water has 15 known phases of ice and several triple points. One of them, at 251 K (−22 °C) and 210 MPa, is where ordinary ice, ice III and liquid water coexist in equilibrium.

paragraphs.heading: Calibrating thermometers
paragraphs.text: Triple-point cells are used to calibrate thermometers. For demanding work they hold a very pure substance, such as hydrogen, argon, mercury or water, picked to match the temperature needed. The purity can reach 99.9999%, nicknamed six nines, meaning only one part in a million is contamination. A set isotopic makeup is used as well, since changes in it shift the triple point a little; for water that standard is called VSMOW. ITS-90 leans on triple-point cells for six of its defined temperatures, using hydrogen, neon, oxygen, argon, mercury and water.

paragraphs.heading: Sea level on Mars
paragraphs.text: During the Mariner 9 mission to Mars, the pressure of water's triple point was used to set a Martian sea level. Today, laser altimetry and gravity measurements are the preferred ways to define heights on Mars.
